title: Primer-lag stitchpad: intermittent warmup and admission shaping
content:
Objective:
Quick explorations into intermittent warmup behavior when admission is shaped into small bursts (microbursts) and its interaction with primer lag (time between first request and steady KV cache hit rate). Notes are rough; used as a running log for ideas to convert into a reproducible harness.

Context / why: 
- We see >2x p95 on client-observed latency for real-client blend when a client sends 4-8 req/s in short spikes with cold KV cache. Hypothesis: primer lag (small warmup traffic) is insufficient to populate KV and kernel warm paths, and admission shaping (coalescing small requests into batches) can exacerbate tail due to serialization and queueing.

Experiment sketch (local harness):
- Model: small transformer-ish (test-model-xsmall) on single A100 sim instance (local emulation).
- Batch window settings: {max_batch_size: 32, batch_timeout_ms: variable} (tried 2ms, 8ms, 20ms).
- Arrival patterns: poisson baseline (mean 5 qps), microburst pattern: base 0.5 qps with bursts: 25 reqs arriving uniformly over 200ms every 30s (to emulate short client spikes).
- Primer sequences: prefix of 16 small priming queries (2 tokens) vs none.
- KV cache policy: unconditional store.
- Measurement: per-request latency (client-observed), server queuing, KV-hit after priming, GPU busy/util.

Runs and quick logs (YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm):
- 2026-01-14 11:03 — baseline poisson (5 qps) + no primer, batch_timeout=8ms
  p50=34ms, p95=89ms, p99=210ms, KV-hit-rate(initial 10s)=8%

- 2026-01-14 11:28 — microburst pattern + no primer, batch_timeout=8ms
  burst window p50=108ms, p95=420ms, p99=980ms, observe queuing spike during bursts; post-burst tail extending ~1.2s for some requests

- 2026-01-15 09:12 — microburst + primer=16 queries before each burst (short warmup) + batch_timeout=8ms
  burst p50=62ms, p95=190ms, p99=520ms, KV-hit-rate(after primer)=72% (first 2s)
  notes: primer reduced p95 by ~2.2x compared to no-primer but did not eliminate p99 long tails; some slow requests still observed due to batch coalescing + cold kernel path (first token generation cost)

- 2026-01-15 10:05 — microburst + primer + batch_timeout=2ms
  burst p50=74ms, p95=210ms, p99=540ms, more small batches -> lower queueing but higher per-token overhead; CPU-side scheduling jitter increased (observed small GC-like pauses in worker process ~10-30ms occasionally)

- 2026-01-16 14:40 — microburst + primer + batch_timeout=20ms
  burst p50=55ms, p95=160ms, p99=760ms, noticed larger coalesced batches gave better p50/p95 but occasionally one request waited the full timeout and then got a big kernel cold path -> p99 increased

Quick ascii-ish telemetry snippets (burst run with primer, batch_timeout=8ms):
- per-second QPS: [0,0,0,8,12,18,7,2,0,0,0,...] (burst concentrated in 3s)
- KV-hit progression in burst window: [5%, 35%, 62%, 75%, 78%, 79%]
- GPU util (sample): [42, 68, 85, 92, 90, 40] (peaks mid-burst then drops)

Rough interpretation:
- Primer sequences that are run immediately before a burst meaningfully increase immediate KV-hit-rate and reduce the mid-tail (p95).
- However, primer does not fully address p99 because large batches and first-token kernel warm paths still cause long-tail events. There are two orthogonal contributors to p99: kernel cold paths (first few tokens) and admission/queueing serialization.
- Increasing batch_timeout helps p50/p95 by allowing more coalescing (amortizing kernel overhead) but can hurt p99 because a straggler will wait longer to be released and may then hit the cold kernel; conversely, very small timeout reduces queuing but increases the number of small expensive kernels.

Immediate actionable ideas to test next:
- Hybrid primer: run 4 warm primers (light) immediately before burst and 12 background primers that run at low rate to keep KV warm globally. Measure whether this reduces p99 beyond the short primer-only strategy.
- Admission tiering: ensure heavy packets in coalesced batch have priority lanes or preemption so a single large batch doesn't stall small low-latency requests. Simulate preemptible batches and measure.
- Kernel pre-warm pool: maintain a tiny pool of pre-warmed execution contexts that can serve first-token quickly; measure extra GPU memory vs latency benefit.
- Adaptive batch_timeout: increase timeout briefly when primer hit-rate is high; reduce when hit-rate low. Implement simple controller and test in harness.

Open questions / anomalies observed:
- Why did batch_timeout=20ms sometimes increase p99 more than 8ms? Hypothesis: a request that enters at t=0 waits 20ms, gets combined into a big batch which triggers a heavier kernel path and the overall kernel scheduling (GPU launch) queue inside the runtime gets blocked by another long-running batch. Need internal traces (task queue timestamps + kernel launch times) to confirm.
- Occasional 10-30ms hiccups on batch_timeout=2ms runs looked like GC or scheduled pauses in python worker. Repro on stripped-down C harness?

Data artifacts to produce for next iteration:
- Per-request trace CSV: timestamp, arrival_delta_ms, queued_ms, kernel_launch_time_ms, model_first_token_ms, total_latency_ms, kv_hit_bool
- Synthetic driver that can toggle primer intensity and background primer rate
- Heatmap generator for p50/p95/p99 vs batch_timeout and primer_size

Short TODOs (prioritized):
